ENT Acting Internship

Rotation survival and performance guide. A phone-first, high-yield study tool for the July ENT acting internship, weighted to the service you are on (head & neck oncology and pediatrics) plus the cross-cutting survival layer that helps on any rotation. Lead with the high-yield number, know the emergencies cold, and look useful in the OR. Personal study notes, not clinical guidance; verify management against current guidelines and your team.

Part

PART I. TIER-1 CRAM AND EMERGENCIES

▸

ENT emergencies card (know these cold)

Emergency Recognize First move
Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate Failed mask + failed intubation, falling sats Front-of-neck airway through the cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid and cricoid cartilage); in children younger than about 12 use needle cricothyrotomy + jet ventilation (the membrane is too small for a surgical cric)
Expanding neck hematoma (post-thyroid/neck/carotid) Swelling, voice change, stridor Open the incision at the bedside to decompress, then definitive control in the OR
Post-tonsillectomy bleed Bleeding, or repeated swallowing in a child (swallowed blood hides volume) ABCs and IV access; most secondary bleeds are POD 5–10; active or significant bleed goes to the OR
Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) “Hot-potato” voice, trismus, uvula pushed away from the bulge Needle aspiration or I&D + antibiotics (adolescents/young adults)
Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA) Young child, neck stiffness, odynophagia; lateral neck film shows widened prevertebral soft tissue CT with contrast; airway watch; drainage; risk is spread to the danger space and mediastinum
Ludwig angina Bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental cellulitis (usually odontogenic), floor-of-mouth elevation, tongue displacement Secure the airway early, IV antibiotics, drainage
ACE-inhibitor angioedema Non-itchy, non-urticarial lip/tongue swelling; can appear at any time on the drug (usually early, sometimes after years) Airway is the priority; it is bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine/antihistamine/steroid are unreliable
Epiglottitis (supraglottitis) Now adult-predominant; muffled voice, drooling, tripod posture; thumbprint sign on lateral neck Do not agitate a suspected pediatric case; secure the airway in the OR; broad antibiotics
Orbital complications of sinusitis Postseptal signs: proptosis, painful or limited eye movement, vision change (vs preseptal lid swelling only) CT; IV antibiotics; subperiosteal/orbital abscess needs drainage
Retrobulbar hematoma (e.g., post-FESS) Proptosis, tense orbit, rising intraocular pressure, vision loss Emergent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss ≥30 dB over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours; (+) Weber to the better ear MRI to rule out retrocochlear disease; oral corticosteroids are an option, and intratympanic steroids should be offered as salvage for incomplete recovery (AAO-HNS SSNHL, 2019)
Auricular hematoma Fluctuant pinna after trauma Drain and bolster to prevent cauliflower ear
Nasal septal hematoma Bluish septal bulge after nasal trauma Drain to prevent septal abscess and saddle-nose deformity
Emergency

Emergency framing. The recurring ENT-call pattern is airway first, then stop the bleeding, then drain the pus. When in doubt about an airway, get to a controlled setting (OR) before it fails.

Master numbers

Audiogram and tuning forks (say Weber/Rinne slowly, it is the most-flubbed pimp):

  • Normal hearing ≤25 dB. An air-bone gap means a conductive component.
  • Weber lateralizes to a conductive ear and away from a sensorineural ear. Rinne: AC > BC is normal or sensorineural; BC > AC is conductive.
  • Carhart notch (~2000 Hz dip in bone conduction) suggests otosclerosis; a 4000 Hz notch is noise-induced; downsloping high-frequency loss is presbycusis.

Antibiotics (stewardship, do not reflexively reach for a macrolide or fluoroquinolone):

Condition First-line Note
Acute otitis media High-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day Amoxicillin-clavulanate if amoxicillin in the prior 30 days, concurrent conjunctivitis, or failure (AAP, 2013); observation an option in select nonsevere cases
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis Offer watchful waiting (preferred, with assured follow-up); if treating, amoxicillin ± clavulanate for 5–7 days Diagnose at >10 days without improvement, or double-worsening (AAO-HNS Adult Sinusitis, updated 2025)
Group A strep pharyngitis Penicillin or amoxicillin Confirm before treating

Pediatric airway sizing: the cricoid (subglottis) is the narrowest fixed, complete ring in young children (classic teaching; in-vivo imaging suggests the glottis is functionally narrowest, a point an attending may probe). Uncuffed ETT size = (age/4) + 4; cuffed ≈ (age/4) + 3.5; depth at the lip ≈ 3 × tube size.

Epistaxis ladder (AAO-HNS Nosebleed, 2020): firm compression + topical vasoconstrictor first, then cautery of an anterior (Kiesselbach/Little’s area) source, then packing; refractory posterior bleeds (sphenopalatine territory, Woodruff plexus) go to sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolization.

Perioperative tonsillectomy: give dexamethasone; do not give routine perioperative antibiotics (AAO-HNS Tonsillectomy, 2019).

Part

PART II. HEAD AND NECK ONCOLOGY

▸

Neck levels I to VII

  • Ia submental; Ib submandibular. II upper jugular, split by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) into IIa (anterior) and IIb (posterior). III mid-jugular; IV lower jugular. V posterior triangle, split into Va/Vb by the horizontal plane at the inferior border of the anterior cricoid arch. VI central compartment (hyoid to suprasternal notch, between the carotids). VII superior mediastinal.
  • Boundaries worth memorizing: the II/III border is the inferior border of the hyoid (the carotid bifurcation is a nearby surgical landmark, not the formal boundary); the III/IV border is the inferior border of the cricoid.
  • Use the AHNS/AAO-HNS (Robbins) classification language; primary sites drain to predictable levels (table below).
Primary site First-echelon nodes Pearl
Oral cavity I to III the oral tongue can skip to III/IV
Oropharynx II to IV (retropharyngeal mainly for posterior-wall/soft-palate primaries) often bilateral; HPV-positive disease classically presents as a cystic level II node
Larynx / hypopharynx II to IV the glottis has sparse lymphatics (late nodal spread, good prognosis); supraglottis and pharynx spread early and bilaterally
Nasopharynx retropharyngeal, then II/V bilateral; EBV-associated

Carotid bifurcation and the great vessels

  • CCA bifurcates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, about C3–C4 (variable, C3–C5). ICA posterolateral, ECA anteromedial.
  • Carotid bulb = proximal ICA = the plaque site; seat of the carotid sinus (baroreceptor, mainly CN IX via the nerve of Hering) and carotid body (chemoreceptor, CN IX and CN X; origin of carotid-body paragangliomas).
  • First ECA branch is the superior thyroid artery; the ICA has no branches in the neck (first is the ophthalmic, intracranial). ECA branches, “Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students”: Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal. The maxillary gives the middle meningeal and the sphenopalatine, the “artery of epistaxis.”

Cranial nerves of the neck (also your cranial-nerve exam)

Nerve Injury sign Where it is at risk
Hypoglossal (XII) Tongue deviates toward the lesion Crosses the ICA/ECA high, about 2 cm above the bifurcation
Vagus (X) / RLN fibers Hoarseness In the carotid sheath; postoperative hoarseness is usually vagal traction/neuropraxia (the cervical RLN is rarely cut) and is mostly transient
Superior laryngeal n. (external br.) Voice fatigue, loss of high pitch (“opera singer’s nerve”) Runs with the superior thyroid artery at the superior pole
Marginal mandibular br. (VII) Asymmetric lower lip and smile High incision or retraction near the mandibular angle
Glossopharyngeal (IX) Dysphagia Very high dissection
Spinal accessory (XI) Trapezius weakness, shoulder drop Posterior triangle, the neck-dissection nerve; splits levels IIa/IIb

Carotid sheath = “VAN”: Vein (IJV, lateral), Artery (carotid, medial), Nerve (vagus, posterior between them). The sympathetic chain runs behind the sheath, so injury there causes Horner syndrome.

Deep neck spaces

  • Retropharyngeal space: between the buccopharyngeal (visceral) fascia and the alar fascia, from the skull base down to about the carina (T4, variable); the site of pediatric retropharyngeal abscess.
  • Danger space: between the alar and prevertebral fascia, running from the skull base to the diaphragm; this is the route to mediastinitis (the high-yield distinction from the retropharyngeal space).
  • Prevertebral space: between the prevertebral fascia and the vertebral bodies, the length of the spine.
  • Parapharyngeal space, divided by the styloid process: pre-styloid holds fat and the deep parotid (the pleomorphic adenoma lives here); post-styloid (carotid space) holds the carotid sheath (ICA, IJV, vagus/CN X, sympathetic chain; CN IX, XI, XII pass only at the skull base), where paragangliomas and schwannomas arise.

Larynx: RLN versus SLN

  • SLN external branch to the cricothyroid muscle: tenses and raises pitch (the “opera singer” nerve); injury causes voice fatigue and loss of high pitch. SLN internal branch is sensory to the supraglottis; injury risks aspiration.
  • RLN supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor (the cord-opener).
  • The classic teaching that an isolated RLN injury leaves the cord paramedian and a combined RLN + SLN injury leaves it intermediate (cadaveric) is the traditional Semon/Wagner-Grossman rule; final cord position is clinically variable, so present it as classic teaching, not a hard fact.

Thyroid and parathyroid landmarks

  • RLN runs in the tracheoesophageal groove; its relationship to the inferior thyroid artery is variable (do not state a fixed deep/superficial rule). The nerve is most at risk near Berry’s ligament at the posterior superior pole.
  • Non-recurrent right inferior laryngeal nerve occurs essentially only on the right, paired with an aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) and dysphagia lusoria.
  • Superior parathyroids come from the 4th pouch (more constant, posterolateral, above the ITA-RLN crossing); inferior parathyroids from the 3rd pouch (with the thymus, more variable). Both parathyroids’ blood supply is predominantly the inferior thyroid artery.

Free flaps for reconstruction

Flap Pedicle Use / safety step
Radial forearm Radial artery + venae comitantes / cephalic vein Thin, pliable lining for oral cavity/oropharynx; Allen test first
Fibula Peroneal artery Workhorse for the mandible (long bone segment); confirm the peroneal is not the dominant leg vessel (exam + CT angiography)
Anterolateral thigh (ALT) Descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery Bulky soft-tissue workhorse
  • Flaps commonly anastomose to ECA branches (superior thyroid or facial) with internal jugular venous outflow (end-to-side IJV, or a branch/comitans vein). Ischemia tolerance is approximate and tissue-dependent (bone tolerates less than fasciocutaneous); do not quote a single hard number.

Cancer staging and HPV (concepts, not cutoffs)

Know the framework, not the centimeters: the exact TNM cutoffs change by AJCC edition, so reason in concepts and look up the current edition for numbers.

Q A
What do T, N, and M describe? T = extent of the primary tumor (size and/or local invasion, by subsite; e.g., the larynx uses cord mobility, not size), N = regional lymph nodes, M = distant metastasis
Which nodal feature most worsens prognosis and upstages N? Extranodal extension (ENE): upstages N (new N3b) in most sites, but not in HPV-positive oropharynx or nasopharynx (still adverse there). ENE or a positive margin is the NCCN high-risk indication for adjuvant chemoradiation; other adverse features generally get radiation alone
Why is HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer staged separately? Distinct biology and a much better prognosis, so it has its own staging (AJCC 8th); p16 immunostaining is the clinical surrogate for HPV
What two exposures drive most non-HPV head and neck SCC? Tobacco and alcohol (synergistic)

Neck dissection types

The named types differ by which non-lymphatic structures (the SCM, IJV, and CN XI) are taken or spared.

Type Nodal levels SCM / IJV / CN XI
Radical (RND) I to V all three removed
Modified radical (MRND) I to V at least one of the three preserved (the goal when oncologically safe)
Selective (SND) only the levels at risk (I to III for oral cavity, often I to IV for oral tongue/floor of mouth; II to IV for larynx/pharynx) all three preserved
Extended RND plus extra node group(s) and/or non-lymphatic structure(s) as needed

Salivary gland tumors

Q A
Most common salivary tumor, and most common parotid tumor? Pleomorphic adenoma (benign; small lifetime risk of malignant transformation)
Most common malignant salivary tumor (overall and in children)? Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Salivary cancer notorious for perineural spread and late distant recurrence? Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Bilateral, benign, in older male smokers? Warthin tumor
Does a smaller gland mean higher malignancy risk? Yes, as a heuristic: parotid ~25% malignant, submandibular ~40 to 50%, and the sublingual highest (~70 to 90%), the exception to memorize

HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer

Q A
Typical patient? Younger, often a nonsmoker; tonsil or base-of-tongue primary
Classic presentation? A painless cystic neck node: an adult “branchial cyst” is cancer until proven otherwise, so image and biopsy, do not just excise
p16 testing caveat? p16 is a valid HPV surrogate only in the oropharynx (confirm with HPV testing elsewhere); p16-positive disease has a better prognosis, though discordant p16-positive/HPV-negative tumors do worse
Part

PART III. PEDIATRIC ENT

▸

Tonsils and adenoids

  • Tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection, Paradise criteria: ≥7 episodes in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years (AAO-HNS Tonsillectomy, 2019). Obstructive sleep-disordered breathing is the other major indication and is now the commonest reason for the operation.
  • Watchful waiting is appropriate for recurrent infection that does not meet Paradise. Give perioperative dexamethasone; avoid routine perioperative antibiotics.

Ear: tubes and effusion

  • Tympanostomy tubes (AAO-HNS, 2022): for recurrent acute otitis media (≥3 in 6 months, or ≥4 in 12 months with one recent), offer tubes only if a middle-ear effusion is present at assessment (do not place if no effusion); for chronic effusion ≥3 months (unilateral or bilateral) with a documented hearing difficulty or other effusion-related symptoms.
  • Otitis media with effusion is otherwise often observed; document hearing.

Pediatric airway and stridor

  • Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of stridor: inspiratory stridor, worse supine and with feeding, usually self-resolving by 12–18 months; severe cases get supraglottoplasty.
  • Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis): the classic viral, subglottic cause (compared with epiglottitis in the table below).
  • Foreign body: sudden choking, asymmetric exam; bronchoscopy.
  • Remember epiglottitis (now rarer in vaccinated children) and bacterial tracheitis on the differential for a toxic child with stridor.
  • The cricoid is the narrowest fixed ring of the pediatric airway (classic teaching; in-vivo imaging suggests the glottis is functionally narrowest), which is why subglottic pathology and tube sizing matter.

The level of obstruction predicts the stridor phase: inspiratory (supraglottic/glottic), biphasic (fixed subglottic), expiratory (intrathoracic/tracheal).

Croup versus epiglottitis

Feature Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) Epiglottitis (supraglottitis)
Cause Parainfluenza (viral) Bacterial; now rare in vaccinated children since Hib immunization, so think H influenzae in the unvaccinated, otherwise strep/staph; increasingly an adult disease
Onset / age Viral URI prodrome (1 to 3 days), then often an abrupt barky cough (classically at night); not fulminant. 6 months to 3 years Rapid (hours), toxic-appearing; any age
Hallmarks Barky/seal cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarse Drooling, dysphagia, tripod/sniffing posture, muffled “hot-potato” voice, high fever; no barky cough
Imaging (only if stable) Steeple sign (subglottic narrowing) on AP neck Thumbprint sign (swollen epiglottis) on lateral neck
First move Cool mist supportive; dexamethasone (any severity); nebulized epinephrine if stridor at rest Do not agitate. Controlled airway: OR with ENT/anesthesia (tracheostomy backup) for unstable or pediatric cases; many adults are observed in the ICU without intubation. Then cultures and IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone, add anti-staph/MRSA cover)

Pediatric subglottic stenosis (Cotton-Myer grade)

Q A
Cotton-Myer grade I? Up to 50% luminal obstruction
Cotton-Myer grade II? 51 to 70% obstruction
Cotton-Myer grade III? 71 to 99% obstruction (a detectable lumen remains)
Cotton-Myer grade IV? No detectable lumen (100%)
Most common cause of acquired subglottic stenosis in a child? Prolonged endotracheal intubation (vs congenital, where the cricoid is malformed)

Pediatric neck masses

A neck mass in a child is congenital, inflammatory, or neoplastic; location and how it moves narrow it fast. Reactive lymphadenopathy is by far the commonest, but a firm, fixed, supraclavicular, or steadily enlarging node (or one with night sweats or weight loss) needs a malignancy workup.

Q A
Midline mass that elevates with tongue protrusion / swallowing? Thyroglossal duct cyst (resect with the central hyoid, the Sistrunk procedure); confirm normal orthotopic thyroid first
Lateral neck mass along the anterior SCM border? Branchial cleft cyst (usually 2nd cleft); often presents when it infects
Soft, compressible, transilluminating mass, often present at birth? A lymphatic malformation (cystic hygroma, classically posterior triangle)
Compressible mass that enlarges with crying/Valsalva? A vascular malformation (venous), or a hemangioma in infancy
Red-flag features that push you toward malignancy workup? Firm, fixed, > 2 cm, supraclavicular, rapidly growing, or with B symptoms (lymphoma, or metastatic in older children)

PART IV. OTOLOGY AND AUDIOLOGY

▸

Ear anatomy

  • External: auricle and EAC (outer cartilaginous third, inner bony two-thirds) to the tympanic membrane (pars tensa below, pars flaccida in the attic above).
  • Middle ear: ossicles malleus to incus to stapes (stapes footplate in the oval window). The facial nerve (tympanic segment) runs above the oval window and is dehiscent in up to half of ears; the chorda tympani (taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue) crosses the middle ear; the stapedius (CN VII) dampens loud sound.
  • Inner ear: cochlea (hearing) and the vestibular labyrinth (balance); the round window is the pressure-release membrane.

High-yield otology

  • Cholesteatoma: keratinizing squamous epithelium, usually an acquired pars flaccida (attic) retraction pocket; locally destructive (erodes ossicles, can cause a labyrinthine fistula or facial palsy); get a CT temporal bone. It is not a neoplasm, despite the name.
  • Otosclerosis: stapes footplate fixation, conductive loss with a Carhart notch (~2000 Hz), often a young adult; treat with observation, a hearing aid, or surgery (stapedotomy, now more common than total stapedectomy).
  • Vertigo: BPPV (brief positional vertigo; the posterior-canal type is Dix-Hallpike positive and treated with the Epley maneuver); Meniere disease (episodic vertigo, low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, aural fullness); vestibular neuritis (acute prolonged vertigo, no hearing loss; with hearing loss it is labyrinthitis); vestibular schwannoma (asymmetric SNHL or tinnitus, get an MRI).
  • Facial nerve palsy: grade with House-Brackmann (I to VI; VI = complete). Bell’s palsy: idiopathic, give oral steroids within 72 hours (antivirals are an adjunct, not monotherapy; AAO-HNS Bell’s Palsy 2013). Ramsay Hunt (zoster oticus): facial palsy plus vesicles (often with SNHL or vertigo), worse prognosis, treat with steroids and antivirals.
Q A
Most common acquired cholesteatoma site? Pars flaccida (attic) retraction pocket
Is cholesteatoma a cancer? No, it is keratinizing squamous epithelium, locally destructive but non-neoplastic
Dix-Hallpike positive, treated with which maneuver? The Epley maneuver (BPPV)
Triad of Meniere disease? Episodic vertigo, low-frequency SNHL, and tinnitus (with aural fullness)
Bell’s palsy first-line? Oral steroids within 72 hours (antivirals as an adjunct)
Ramsay Hunt versus Bell’s? Ramsay Hunt has vesicles (zoster) and a worse prognosis; treat with steroids + antivirals

PART V. RHINOLOGY AND SINUS

▸

Sinus drainage and the OMC

  • The ostiomeatal complex (OMC) is the common drainage pathway of the maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal sinuses into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoid and sphenoid drain to the superior meatus / sphenoethmoidal recess; the nasolacrimal duct drains to the inferior meatus.

FESS danger zones (where you can cause real harm)

  • Lamina papyracea: the thin medial orbital wall; a breach enters orbital fat (the most commonly injured orbital structure).
  • Anterior ethmoidal artery: crosses the skull base, often in a mesentery below the roof; a retracted stump bleeds into the orbit (an orbital hematoma, an emergency).
  • Cribriform plate and lateral lamella: the thinnest skull-base bone and the commonest iatrogenic CSF-leak site (the Keros I to III types describe how deep the olfactory fossa sits).
  • Sphenoid posterolateral wall: the internal carotid artery and optic nerve; an Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell can carry the optic nerve into the posterior ethmoid.
Q A
Keros type I? Shallow olfactory fossa (1 to 3 mm); lowest skull-base injury risk
Keros type II? 4 to 7 mm (most common)
Keros type III? Deep (8 to 16 mm); a long thin lateral lamella, so the highest CSF-leak / skull-base injury risk

High-yield rhinology

  • Chronic rhinosinusitis is ≥12 weeks of cardinal symptoms plus objective confirmation (endoscopy or CT), with (CRSwNP) or without nasal polyps. Samter triad: aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, asthma, and nasal polyps.
  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: an adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass fed chiefly by the internal maxillary artery (via its sphenopalatine branch); it is vascular, so do not biopsy it in clinic, image first.
  • Inverted papilloma: unilateral, can harbor a squamous cell carcinoma (~5 to 10%), so excise it completely at its bony attachment.
Fungal sinusitis Setting Key point
Acute invasive immunocompromised, diabetic ketoacidosis an emergency: angioinvasive (mucormycosis, aspergillus), needs urgent surgical debridement + IV antifungals
Chronic invasive / granulomatous indolent, often immunocompetent slow tissue invasion; surgery plus antifungals
Allergic fungal (AFRS) atopic, younger, immunocompetent non-invasive; nasal polyps with eosinophilic “allergic mucin”; surgery + corticosteroids (perioperative oral, then maintenance topical); systemic antifungals not routine
Fungal ball (mycetoma) older, immunocompetent, one sinus (usually maxillary) non-invasive tangle of hyphae; cured by surgical removal
Q A
What drains into the middle meatus through the OMC? The maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal sinuses
Most common iatrogenic CSF-leak site in sinus surgery? The cribriform / lateral lamella (graded by the Keros types)
Samter triad? Aspirin sensitivity, asthma, nasal polyps
Adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass: diagnosis and a key rule? Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma; do not biopsy (vascular), image first
Which structures sit in the sphenoid posterolateral wall? The internal carotid artery and optic nerve (watch for an Onodi cell)
Part

PART VI. LARYNGOLOGY AND AIRWAY

▸

Larynx anatomy

  • Cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (the only complete ring), paired arytenoids, and the epiglottis. Subsites: supraglottis, glottis (the cords), and subglottis.
  • Innervation (see Part II): the RLN supplies all intrinsics except the cricothyroid; the SLN external branch supplies the cricothyroid; the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor.

Hoarseness and benign lesions

  • Vocal cord nodules: bilateral, at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds, from voice overuse (“singer’s nodules”); treat with voice therapy.
  • Polyps (often unilateral), Reinke edema (diffuse, in smokers), recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (HPV 6 and 11), leukoplakia (a clinical finding that mandates biopsy, since it may harbor dysplasia), and vocal cord paralysis (an RLN problem until proven otherwise, so image the full nerve course).
  • Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP): HPV 6 and 11. Juvenile-onset is more aggressive and multifocal (vertical transmission at birth); adult-onset is often more solitary. Treat with serial surgical debulking (microdebrider or laser), avoid tracheostomy when possible (risk of distal seeding); malignant transformation is rare. HPV vaccination lowers incidence.

Laryngeal cancer (high-yield)

  • Squamous cell carcinoma, driven by smoking and alcohol. Glottic cancers present early with hoarseness and have a good prognosis (the cords have sparse lymphatics). Supraglottic cancers present later and spread to nodes early.
Q A
The only complete cartilage ring of the airway? The cricoid
Where do vocal cord nodules form? The junction of the anterior and middle thirds, bilaterally
Virus behind recurrent respiratory papillomatosis? HPV 6 and 11
Why do glottic cancers have a good prognosis? Early hoarseness plus sparse cord lymphatics (late nodal spread)
A new unilateral vocal cord paralysis means what until proven otherwise? An RLN lesion along its course (image from skull base to mediastinum)
Part

PART VII. FACIAL PLASTICS AND TRAUMA

▸

Facial trauma

  • Nasal fracture: the most common facial fracture; always check for and drain a septal hematoma.
  • Mandible fracture: suspect it with malocclusion; fractures are often multiple (the ring tends to break twice); the angle and condyle are common sites.
  • Orbital blowout: the floor (maxillary) or medial wall (lamina papyracea); watch for inferior rectus entrapment with vertical diplopia (and the oculocardiac reflex, especially in children with a “white-eyed” trapdoor fracture).
  • Zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture (the older “tripod” term undercounts its four buttresses) and the Le Fort I/II/III midface patterns (all Le Fort fractures cross the pterygoid plates).
  • Temporal bone fracture: longitudinal (the more common; conductive loss, ossicular injury) versus transverse (more SNHL, vertigo, and facial palsy); the modern outcome-predictive split is otic-capsule sparing vs violating. Look for Battle sign, hemotympanum, and CSF otorrhea.

Skin cancer and reconstruction

  • Basal cell carcinoma is the most common (rolled pearly border, rarely metastasizes); squamous cell carcinoma can spread perineurally; melanoma is staged by depth. Mohs surgery spares tissue on the face.
  • Reconstruct up the ladder (secondary intention, primary closure, skin graft, local flap, free flap); cleft lip and palate repair overlaps with pediatrics.
Q A
Most common facial fracture, and what must you check? Nasal bone; check for and drain a septal hematoma
Which temporal bone fracture more often causes SNHL and facial palsy? Transverse (longitudinal tends to cause conductive loss)
What do all Le Fort fractures share? They cross the pterygoid plates
Most common skin cancer of the face? Basal cell carcinoma
Orbital floor blowout sign with vertical diplopia? Inferior rectus entrapment
Part

PART VIII. OR SURVIVAL AND AI REBUILD

▸

The behaviors that are the evaluation

  • Suction without obscuring the field, follow suture, cut on the flat of the scissors at the surgeon’s knot, retract steadily, and load needles correctly. Anticipate the next move. These intangibles are most of what an acting intern is graded on.
  • Know the case before you scrub: indication, the steps, and the one or two numbers you might be asked.

Instruments and suture

Instrument Role
DeBakey forceps atraumatic pickups (never grab a vessel with toothed forceps)
Castroviejo needle driver / scissors micro instruments (the same ones used under the scope for microvascular work)
Bulldog clamp soft, atraumatic vessel occlusion
Potts scissors extend an arteriotomy or venotomy
Freer / Cottle elevator raise mucoperichondrial and subperiosteal flaps (septoplasty, sinus, ear)
Weitlaner / Gelpi self-retaining retractors
  • Microvascular suture: permanent monofilament (nylon or Prolene) on a tapered needle, stepping down to 8-0, 9-0, 10-0 for free-flap vessels. Double-armed, parachute the posterior wall, lay throws flat with constant tension, back-bleed before the final tie, then confirm flow.

The two genuine transfer clusters from vascular

  1. The carotid and neck block. A carotid exposure is anatomically a neck dissection: the bifurcation, the ICA/ECA, the cranial nerves above, the sheath (VAN), and the IJV (the free-flap recipient vein).
  2. Fine-tissue and monofilament skill. Atraumatic handling under loupes or the scope, no-touch intima, and suction as a skill.

Knots and graduated responsibility

  • Practice nightly: a flat, square, snug two-handed knot and an instrument tie, both without looking; then needle loading and a simple closure.
  • Earn responsibility a rung at a time, asked in a calm moment, not mid-anastomosis: camera/suction, then retract, then cut, then first-assist, then a few ties, then close skin. After you do something, ask what to change next time.
Part

PART IX. SELF-TEST: PIMP Q&A

▸

Quiz mode is on: tap a blurred answer to reveal it.

Cover the answer column to self-test. This is a scaffold of the questions actually asked on the service; verify each answer as you study.

Emergencies and airway

Q A
Landmark for an emergency surgical airway? The cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage
Why avoid a surgical cricothyrotomy in a young child? The cricoid is the narrowest point and the membrane is tiny; use a needle cric + jet ventilation
Typical timing of a secondary post-tonsillectomy bleed? POD 5–10 (eschar separation), peak around POD 7
Which way does the uvula deviate in a peritonsillar abscess? Away from the abscess
Why does ACE-inhibitor angioedema not respond to the usual allergy cocktail? It is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated; protect the airway
Audiometric definition of sudden SNHL? ≥30 dB over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours; get an MRI
First imaging for sudden SNHL, and what are you ruling out? MRI, to exclude retrocochlear pathology (vestibular schwannoma)

Head and neck anatomy

Q A
First branch of the ECA? Superior thyroid artery (SALFOPMS)
ICA branches in the neck? None (the first is the ophthalmic, intracranial)
Carotid sheath contents? VAN: carotid (medial), IJV (lateral), vagus (posterior between them)
What splits neck level II into IIa and IIb? The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
Where does the danger space run? Skull base to the diaphragm (between alar and prevertebral fascia)
Only abductor of the vocal cords? Posterior cricoarytenoid (RLN)
Blood supply to both parathyroid glands? Predominantly the inferior thyroid artery
Five terminal (parotid-plexus) branches of the facial nerve? Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical (also the proximal posterior auricular branch)

Pediatrics

Q A
Most common congenital cause of stridor? Laryngomalacia (inspiratory, worse supine/feeding)
Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy? ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5/year × 2 years, ≥3/year × 3 years
Tube criteria for recurrent AOM? ≥3 episodes in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months with effusion (AAO-HNS, 2022)
Narrowest part of the pediatric airway? Classic answer the cricoid (narrowest fixed ring); note imaging suggests the glottis is functionally narrowest
Steeple sign and a barky cough? Croup (subglottic)
Part

PART X. ROTATION PLAN

▸

Daily rhythm

  • Pre-round on your patients: airway, drains, flap checks (color, capillary refill, Doppler signal, temperature), pain, intake/output, voice and swallow.
  • In the OR, scrub every case you can, know the steps, and own suction and retraction.
  • In clinic, learn the headlight, scope, and microscope exams and how to read an audiogram.
  • At night, 20 minutes: knots, then one section of this guide, then tomorrow’s cases.

Resources

Resource Use it for
Pasha, Otolaryngology Clinical Reference Guide fast high-yield review and pimp prep
ENT Secrets question-and-answer reinforcement
AAO-HNSF Primary Care Otolaryngology Handbook clinic-level basics
Current AAO-HNS clinical practice guidelines the authority for management questions (cite the year)
Netter atlases the anatomy plates behind the diagrams here

Micro-habits

  • Each night, mark off the day’s cards and read one new section.
  • After every case, write down the one fact you were asked and did not know.
